results.Proposed_Explanation: Massachusetts MassPAT reporting under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) covers dispensing of Schedule II through V controlled substances pursuant to a prescription and dispensing of any drug the Commissioner has designated an additional drug under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(8). Pregabalin is Massachusetts Schedule V, because 105 CMR 700.002(E) adopts the Schedule V list in 21 CFR 1308.15, where pregabalin appears. Gabapentin is a Massachusetts Schedule VI drug that the Commissioner has designated as a reportable additional drug, and the Drug Control Program instructs pharmacies to submit all gabapentin dispensations to the PMP. Both are therefore reportable on the basis of the drug alone, whatever the indication. An ordinary CMEA retail sale of pseudoephedrine is not reportable to MassPAT, because it is an over-the-counter transaction in a scheduled listed chemical product under 21 CFR part 1314 rather than a prescription dispensing of a Schedule II-V controlled substance or an additional drug.

results.Problem: No legal defect. Methylphenidate is Schedule II at 21 CFR 1308.12(d)(4) and Massachusetts Schedule II by incorporation at 105 CMR 700.002(B). The decisive provision is M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4), which I read in full: after providing for the patient-requested lesser quantity it states 'provided, however, that only the same pharmacy that originally dispensed the lesser quantity shall dispense the remaining portion.' The second pharmacy therefore has no lawful route to the balance on day 20 or any other day, so keyed answer B is correct. The federal layer agrees rather than conflicting: 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(1) conditions the patient-requested pathway on state law permitting it, and 1306.13(b)(2) sets an outer limit of 30 days from the date written, which is a deadline and not a transfer permission. Distractor A is correctly unkeyed on two independent grounds, because a Schedule II partial-fill balance is not a refill and because s. 23(b) bars refilling a Schedule II prescription at all. Distractor C is correctly unkeyed because nothing converts an undispensed balance into a new prescription; s. 23(a) makes the prescription invalid 30 days after issuance and s. 18(d3/4) closes the remainder window at the same point. Distractor D is correctly unkeyed because dispensing does not reschedule a drug. The keyed option's phrase 'belongs to the original pharmacy's partial-fill record' is loose as drafting, since the operative reason is the statutory same-pharmacy restriction rather than a records concept, but it is not legally wrong and it does not make another option defensible. The linked rule MA-CII-PARTIAL-PATIENT reproduces the 5-day and 30-day figures correctly. results.Problem: The keyed answer B is correct. 21 CFR 1314.20(a) caps a regulated seller at 3.6 grams of pseudoephedrine base per customer per calendar day without regard to the number of transactions, so a single 4.0 gram request is barred by the daily ceiling. results.Problem: No legal defect. The Massachusetts quantity framework is M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d), which caps other Schedule II or III prescriptions at a 30-day supply per filling but permits up to a 90-day supply on a single filling for '(i) the treatment of opioid use disorder, including, but not limited to, buprenorphine.' Distractor B is correctly unkeyed twice over, because not every opioid-related product is Schedule II and because Schedule III prescriptions may carry refills under 21 CFR 1306.22(a). results.Problem: No legal defect in the keyed sequence. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) fixes all four events and their order. The patient's request is the predicate and precedes the reduced initial quantity, which is choice B. The initial partial dispensing follows and 'shall be filled not more than 5 days after the prescription issue date', which is choice D. The patient then returns for the balance, and 'only the same pharmacy that originally dispensed the lesser quantity shall dispense the remaining portion', which is choice A. The completing dispensing 'must be filled not later than 30 days after the prescription issue date', which is choice C, and this is congruent with 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(2) and with the 30-day validity of a Schedule II prescription under s. 23(a). The keyed order B, D, A, C is therefore correct and every factual predicate in every option is an accurate statement of current Massachusetts law, including the 5-day figure, which I confirmed is a real statutory requirement rather than a narrative flourish. The item nevertheless fails the companion realism review, because the correct order is recoverable from the temporal wording of the options without any Massachusetts law; that is a construction defect, not a legal error, and it is recorded in the realism record. One cross-reference observation outside this tranche's scope: MA-Q-0014 places a patient-requested partial fill of Dexedrine 'at this pharmacy 12 days after issue', which cannot satisfy the 5-day initial dispensing requirement in s. 18(d3/4); that neighbouring item's fact pattern should be checked by whoever owns it.
